requirement_title: Add ExcludeFromCodeCoverage attribute to generated code.
requirement_text:
# REQ-2297: Add ExcludeFromCodeCoverage attribute to generated code.

Source: https://github.com/MessagePack-CSharp/MessagePack-CSharp/issues/2297
Type: feature

## Requirement

MessagePack generated code is not decorated with the `ExcludeFromCodeCoverage` attribute. Because it is very hard to write good coverage for generated MessagePack code, it may skew coverage numbers, especially on large projects with a lot of generated code.

Solution requested: "I would like all generated code to be decorated with ExcludeFromCodeCoverage attribute.  I do not feel like a setting is needed, but setting would be fine to have too."

Alternatives considered by the author: none; "it is close to impossible to write good coverage for generated code as it covers many edge cases."

## Acceptance criteria

- All generated code is decorated with `ExcludeFromCodeCoverage`.
- No new setting or option is required to get the attribute. ("I do not feel like a setting is needed")
- An opt-out setting would be acceptable but is optional. ("setting would be fine to have too")
- The generated code still compiles on every supported target framework (the attribute must exist there or be conditionally emitted). (derived)
- Existing verified generator snapshots are updated to include the attribute. (derived)

## Notes from discussion

- b-kurczynski-dl suggests a coverage-tool workaround instead: exclude `obj\\.*\.g\.cs$` in the `dotnet-coverage` settings XML.
- armadavalor offers a PR: add `[global::System.Diagnostics.CodeAnalysis.ExcludeFromCodeCoverage]` (and possibly `GeneratedCode`) to the types emitted by the templates under `src/MessagePack.SourceGenerator/Transforms/` (formatters, string-key formatters, enum/union formatters, resolvers), update the verified snapshots, no setting. Asks AArnott whether he would accept it or prefer to point users at coverage-tool configuration. No maintainer reply in the thread.
- Ambiguity driver: scope (all generated types vs formatters only) and setting (unconditional vs opt-out) are both open.
verdict_reason: verified high finding(s) backed by receipts: requirement-tests-1, logic-edge-1

checked.what: Existing SourceGenerator tests on head: 169/169 passed, 0 failed
Existing SourceGenerator tests on base: 167/167 passed, 0 failed
Receipts/ExcludeFromCodeCoverageGeneratedCodeTests.cs: requirement test fails on head: 1/2 failed
Receipts/ExcludeFromCodeCoverageOnLegacyTargetsTests.cs: edge-case test fails on head: 2/2 failed
Receipts/ExcludeFromCodeCoverageEdgeCaseTests.cs: edge-case test fails on head: 3/3 failed
Regeneration: 222/222 generated files verified by 89 passing snapshot tests on head
Reading B built as review/ju26-issue-2297/B (380e7af4): builds and the SourceGenerator tests pass (attempt 1 of 2)

findings.claim: The requirement says all generated code gets `ExcludeFromCodeCoverage`. The derived criterion allows conditional emission only where the attribute does not exist. The change wraps every attribute in `#if !NETSTANDARD2_0 && !NETFRAMEWORK`. But `System.Diagnostics.CodeAnalysis.ExcludeFromCodeCoverageAttribute` does exist, with AttributeTargets.Class, in .NET Framework 4.0+ and in netstandard2.0. So consumers building for net4x or netstandard2.0 (a large share of MessagePack users, including libraries) get no attribute on any generated formatter or resolver, and the requirement is not met for them.

receipt_plan.detail: Run Receipts.GeneratedTests.ExcludeFromCodeCoverageOnLegacyTargetsTests.GeneratedTypesAreExcludedEvenWhenLegacyTargetSymbolDefined (NETFRAMEWORK and NETSTANDARD2_0). It drives the generator with that preprocessor symbol and checks every generated class symbol carries the attribute. Expected to fail on head. The same guard appears in EnumTemplate.tt:8, UnionTemplate.tt:10, StringKeyFormatterTemplate.tt:18, ResolverTemplate.tt:14/31/48 and CompositeResolverTemplate.tt:7/35.

findings.claim: Adding `[ExcludeFromCodeCoverage]` unconditionally to the generated half of the user's own `partial` resolver class breaks existing code. Inputs: `[GeneratedMessagePackResolver]` or `[CompositeResolver(...)]` on a `partial class` that the user already marked `[ExcludeFromCodeCoverage]`, which is the obvious thing to do for a resolver class. `ExcludeFromCodeCoverageAttribute` is `AllowMultiple = false`, so on net5+/netcoreapp targets the merged declaration carries the attribute twice and fails with CS0579. Code that compiled on base no longer compiles. The generator does not check whether the user's declaration already has the attribute.

receipt_plan.detail: Run ExcludeFromCodeCoverageEdgeCaseTests.UserResolverAlreadyExcludedFromCoverage_StillCompiles. Its source is `[GeneratedMessagePackResolver][System.Diagnostics.CodeAnalysis.ExcludeFromCodeCoverage] partial class MyResolver {}` with SkipGeneratedSourcesCheck and no expected diagnostics. Base passes; head fails with CS0579 in the generated MyResolver file. The same applies to CompositeResolverTemplate.tt:7.

findings.claim: The guard `#if !NETSTANDARD2_0 && !NETFRAMEWORK` drops the attribute on netstandard2.0 and .NET Framework, which are the most common library targets. `System.Diagnostics.CodeAnalysis.ExcludeFromCodeCoverageAttribute` exists in netstandard2.0 and in .NET Framework 4.0+, so the condition is too broad. On those targets no generated formatter or resolver is excluded from coverage, so 'all generated code is decorated' does not hold. The requirement only allows conditional emission where the attribute does not exist.

receipt_plan.detail: Run ExcludeFromCodeCoverageEdgeCaseTests.GeneratedResolverIsExcludedFromCoverage_WhenTargetDefinesSymbol("NETSTANDARD2_0") and ("NETFRAMEWORK"). Each drives CSharpGeneratorDriver with parse options defining that symbol and asserts that the MyResolver symbol has ExcludeFromCodeCoverageAttribute. On head the attribute is preprocessed away, so the test fails. The same guard appears in every template.

hunches.claim: The attribute is wrapped in `#if !NETSTANDARD2_0 && !NETFRAMEWORK`, so generated code is not decorated when a user project targets netstandard2.0 or .NET Framework. Those targets are common for MessagePack consumers. The requirement says all generated code gets the attribute, and ExcludeFromCodeCoverage exists on net461+ and netstandard2.0, so the guard looks unnecessary. The same guard also skips net472 and net48 projects.

receipt_plan.detail: Run the generator snapshot tests with a netstandard2.0 or net472 compilation and inspect the output. Alternatively compile a sample that defines NETSTANDARD2_0 and check that the formatter has no ExcludeFromCodeCoverage. Then remove the guard and compile for netstandard2.0 to confirm the attribute resolves.

hunches.claim: Generated output now contains `#if`/`#endif` preprocessor lines at column 0 inside nested type bodies. The `TransformUtilities` change from `{` to `{\r\n` alters the whitespace of every nested-type output, whether or not the attribute is involved. This changes the checked-in snapshots for all nested types, which users who snapshot or check in generator output will see. The `#if` lines also do not indent consistently with the surrounding code.

receipt_plan.detail: Rerun the snapshot tests for types with generic constraints. Confirm the diff is limited to the added attribute lines and the newline after `{`. Check that no snapshot differs only in whitespace unrelated to the attribute.

hunches.claim: The attribute was added to the resolver types, the FormatterCache and GetFormatterHelper nested types, and the formatters. The `.tt` and `.cs` pairs appear to stay in sync. However, `CompositeResolverTemplate.cs` and `.tt` add the attribute to partial classes the user declares. If the user's own part of that partial class already carries an attribute or declares a conflicting one, this could cause friction. ExcludeFromCodeCoverage has AllowMultiple=false, so a duplicate would produce CS0579 in the user's build.

receipt_plan.detail: Compile a user-declared `[ExcludeFromCodeCoverage] partial class MyResolver` annotated with `[CompositeResolver]` against the generated part. Expect CS0579 on the duplicate attribute, and assert there is no compile error.

hunches.claim: The change does not cover every generated type. Types emitted via other paths, such as the nesting partial types from EmitNestingTypesAndNamespaces, the `GetFormatterHelper` static class (decorated only in the ResolverTemplate), and any other helper or attribute emission, are not all decorated. The new test only asserts that the attribute appears at least once per file, not on every type. A file containing an undecorated type would still pass.

receipt_plan.detail: Remove the attribute from one of two types in a multi-type generated file, for example FormatterCache<T> in ResolverTemplate.tt. Run CodeCoverageExclusionTests and check whether the mutant survives, since the test only checks per-file presence and that every attribute occurrence is guarded.

hunches.claim: An unrelated behavioural change to the nesting-type emitter appears in the diff: the writer emits `{\r\n` instead of `{` when constraints exist. It alters generated output for constrained nested generics and is not required by the coverage attribute. It is in an area with many recent fixes ([L4]), so it carries regression risk and has no dedicated test.

receipt_plan.detail: Rerun the generator snapshot tests, especially the nested generic types with constraints. Check that the snapshot diffs for them are limited to the added newline and the attribute.

hunches.claim: The new tests never compile the generated output. A guard that is wrong, or an attribute emitted where it does not exist, would still pass, so the 'compiles on every supported target framework' criterion has no test. The tests only check strings, and RunGeneratorAsync discards the generator and compilation diagnostics.

receipt_plan.detail: tests/MessagePack.SourceGenerator.Tests/CodeCoverageExclusionTests.cs:23 swap-boolean: change Guard to '#if NETSTANDARD2_0' and the template guard to match, or emit an invalid attribute name; expected to survive because the tests only do string matching and never compile or check diagnostics.

hunches.claim: The guard test checks that the attribute is wrapped in '#if !NETSTANDARD2_0 && !NETFRAMEWORK', but the same condition is duplicated as a constant in the test, so the test only compares the template to itself. A wrong symbol, such as the real NET Framework define being NETFRAMEWORK versus NET48, would not be detected. The tests also run against one default target framework, so the guarded-out branch is never exercised.

receipt_plan.detail: Compile the generated output with preprocessor symbols NETSTANDARD2_0 and NETFRAMEWORK defined, against a reference set lacking ExcludeFromCodeCoverage, and assert zero errors.

hunches.claim: The TransformUtilities change from '{' to '{\r\n' for nested types with constraints has no targeted test. The new tests contain no nested type with generic constraints. The change matters because a '#if' directive following a constrained nesting type's '{' needs to start on its own line. Reverting the line would not fail any new test.

receipt_plan.detail: src/MessagePack.SourceGenerator/Transforms/TransformUtilities.cs:58 delete-statement: revert '{\r\n' -> '{'; expected to survive in CodeCoverageExclusionTests because TestSource has no nested generic-constrained types. Only the snapshot tests, if they have such a case, would catch it.

hunches.claim: The test asserts only that the attribute appears and is guarded, not that each generated type carries it. The attribute count equals the guarded count, but a file with several types (resolver, FormatterCache, GetFormatterHelper) passes if just one is decorated. The check 'Contains(ExcludeAttribute)' is per file, not per type. Removing the attribute from the nested FormatterCache or GetFormatterHelper in the resolver templates would not fail either test.

receipt_plan.detail: src/MessagePack.SourceGenerator/Transforms/ResolverTemplate.tt:45 delete-statement: remove the attribute from the GetFormatterHelper class; expected to survive because the resolver file still contains the attribute on the resolver class, so the Contains and count checks still pass.

hunches.claim: The README says the attribute is "only emitted for targets where it is available (not `netstandard2.0` or .NET Framework)". That is factually wrong: ExcludeFromCodeCoverageAttribute is available on both. The doc documents the coverage gap as a platform limitation instead of a choice.

receipt_plan.detail: Compare with the API docs for System.Diagnostics.CodeAnalysis.ExcludeFromCodeCoverageAttribute, which list .NET Framework 4.0+ and .NET Standard 2.0. Compiling `[System.Diagnostics.CodeAnalysis.ExcludeFromCodeCoverage] class C {}` against net472 or netstandard2.0 reference assemblies succeeds.

hunches.claim: The attribute is only emitted under `#if !NETSTANDARD2_0 && !NETFRAMEWORK`, so the requirement 'all generated code is decorated' is met only for some target frameworks. The guard is a judgement call about what 'all' means. It also relies on the consuming project defining those preprocessor symbols, which holds for SDK-style projects. The README documents the limitation.

receipt_plan.detail: Compare the guard in all templates with the requirement's 'attribute must exist there or be conditionally emitted'. Confirm that netstandard2.0 and net472 consumers compile, and decide whether they should be excluded from coverage some other way.

hunches.claim: The README note is placed in the custom-formatter mixing section, just before the MagicOnion section. It is not near the source generator documentation, and it says 'All generated formatters and resolvers' while omitting the netstandard2.0 impact on coverage tools. The docs placement is questionable.

receipt_plan.detail: Read the README section around line 1636 and check whether it covers the source generator, or whether a dedicated generator section should hold this note.

refused.what: Choosing between reading A and reading B of REQ-2297
refused.why: The AI will not pick: 3 of 3 independent readers found two readings: A: Unconditionally add [ExcludeFromCodeCoverage] to every type the source generator emits (formatters, enum/union formatters, resolvers, string-key formatters, etc.), with no setting; B: Add the attribute to all generated types by default, plus provide an opt-out setting (e.g. MSBuild property or MessagePackKnownFormatter/GeneratorOptions flag) to disable it; the requirement says: 'I would like all generated code to be decorated with ExcludeFromCodeCoverage attribute. I do not feel like a setting is needed, but setting would be fine to have too'. Reading A: Unconditionally add [ExcludeFromCodeCoverage] to every type the source generator emits (formatters, enum/union formatters, resolvers, string-key formatters, etc.), with no setting. Code: Edit all templates under Transforms/ to emit the attribute on every generated type, always, with no MSBuild property or option; update all snapshots. Reading B: Add the attribute to all generated types by default, plus provide an opt-out setting (e.g. MSBuild property or MessagePackKnownFormatter/GeneratorOptions flag) to disable it. Code: Adds a new public configuration option, reads it in the generator, and conditionally emits the attribute in templates; the other reading adds no option. Which one ships is a product decision, not a correctness question; both branches are built and reviewed with their own receipts, and a named human merges one.

residual_risk: This change touches 237 files (222 generated) in codegen-templates, tests; the highest routed risk is 7/10. 14 file(s) were routed for deep review, 1 for light review and 222 to the regeneration check. The existing source generator tests ran on head: 169 of 169 passed, 0 failed. 12 unverified hunch(es) remain without an executed receipt. It touches risky areas (codegen-templates), so a human must sign off. 5 thing(s) were not checked, including mutation testing; generated formatter bytes (source generator output, base vs head); compatibility byte diff (base vs head serialized bytes). By signing off, the signer accepts any defect that only those unchecked paths would have revealed. The change is blocked; signing off is not offered until the blocker is fixed.
